opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fascinating phenomenon, and it says a lot about what these models really are. If you ask a model to "pick a random number between one and ten," you'd hope for something close to uniform. Instead you get seven a striking amount of the time. If you ask for a random name, a random city, or a random job, the answers cluster around a very small set of choices.

I think there are a few reasons layered on top of each other.

The first is that pretraining teaches the model to imitate human-written text, and humans themselves are bad at being random. When people are asked for a random number, they also over-pick seven, avoid round numbers, and avoid the extremes. So the model has learned the human distribution of "what people say when asked to be random," not actual randomness. It is reproducing our collective bias, and in fact amplifying it.

That amplification is the second piece. The model tends to concentrate probability mass on the most typical answer, because that's what minimizes loss on average. Whatever is slightly more common in the data becomes much more dominant in the output.

The third piece, and I think the most important one, is post-training: instruction tuning, RLHF, preference optimization. These steps reward answers that annotators or reward models judge as good, safe, and helpful. They really sharpen the distribution. The model becomes more confident and more homogeneous, so you lose a lot of the diversity that was still present in the base model. People sometimes call this mode collapse. Base models are often noticeably more diverse than their aligned counterparts.

Finally, there's a conceptual gap. Generating a sample from a distribution and describing what a random sample looks like are two different things. When you ask a model a question, it's essentially answering "what is the most plausible response to this prompt?" Most plausible and random are almost opposites. The model doesn't have an internal coin to flip. It only has its learned sense of what text usually comes next.

Why does this matter beyond random numbers? The same mechanism shows up when you ask for a story about a doctor, a scientist, or a family, or for creative ideas. You get the most stereotypical version again and again. That's a fairness problem, and it's also a creativity and pluralism problem. If millions of people are using the same few models, we risk homogenizing human thought and expression around whatever the model considers the default.

So to me it highlights a real research need. We should think about alignment not only as making models helpful and harmless, but also as preserving diversity and pluralistic values. We need to better understand what's lost in post-training, and design methods that keep the richness of the underlying distribution instead of collapsing it onto a single "safe" answer.

r001.rationale: It says pretraining teaches models to imitate human-written text and that they reproduce and amplify the human biases in those patterns.

r002.rationale: It explains that post-training rewards answers people or reward models prefer, sharpening the distribution and reducing diversity toward more homogeneous outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at something fundamental about what these models actually are. When you ask a language model for a random number, you're asking for something that, by definition, shouldn't depend on anything else. But the model isn't sampling from a uniform distribution over numbers. It's sampling from the distribution of what humans wrote when they were asked, or pretended to be asked, for a random number. And it turns out humans are terrible at this. We love seven. We avoid round numbers because they don't feel random. We cluster in the middle of whatever range we're given. So the model inherits all of that.

And I think that's the key point. These models are, in a very deep sense, mirrors of the data they were trained on, and the data is full of human biases, human quirks, human laziness. So when the output looks skewed or stereotypical, that's not a bug in some separate component. It's the model doing exactly what it was optimized to do, which is predict the most likely continuation given the patterns it has seen.

What makes it tricky is that the model has no concept of what "random" means as a goal. It has a statistical association between the word "random" and certain outputs. There's no internal mechanism saying, okay, now I need to go flip a coin. It's all one and the same next-token prediction. And this generalizes well beyond numbers. If you ask it to name a doctor or a nurse, or to describe a typical family, you get the same phenomenon. The model collapses toward the mode of the training distribution, which is often the stereotype, because the stereotype is literally the most frequent pattern.

The other thing I'd add is that the decoding procedure matters a lot. Most of the time we're not sampling from the full distribution. We're using greedy decoding, or low temperature, or nucleus sampling, all of which push the model toward the high-probability region and prune away the tail. So even if the model has some probability mass on the number 83, the decoding step tends to flatten that out. We're actively making the model less diverse than it already is.

So to me this is really a lens into the bigger problem. We often talk as if these models have knowledge, or intent, or some kind of understanding, but moments like this remind us that what they really have is a very compressed, somewhat lossy summary of human text. And if we want them to behave differently, whether that's being genuinely random or being fair, we have to build that in deliberately. It doesn't come for free from scale.

r001.rationale: It says the model learns from human-written data and inherits its biases and quirks, so its outputs reflect the patterns in that training data.

r002.rationale: It says decoding methods can favor high-probability outputs, but does not state that post-training concentrates probabilities on stereotypical answers people prefer.

astra-6.text:
I think it illustrates that language models learn what people tend to say, which is different from learning how to sample randomly. If you ask for a random number, the model is still predicting a plausible response based on patterns in text. Some numbers may show up more often in that context, so they become more likely answers.

And that same mechanism can produce stereotypes. If certain occupations or traits are repeatedly associated with particular groups in the training data, those associations can shape the answer, even when your question doesn’t call for them. A neutral prompt doesn’t necessarily give you a neutral distribution of responses. The model brings the patterns it has learned into that interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says the model learns patterns in its training text, including numbers and group-trait associations that appear more often, making those responses more likely.

r002.rationale: It does not mention post-training or that user preferences further concentrate output probabilities on stereotypical answers.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it highlights the gap between predicting language and actually understanding what we’re asking for. When we ask for a random number, we might expect every number in a given range to have an equal chance. But a language model is predicting what text is likely to come next, based on patterns in its training data. Some numbers appear much more often than others, and certain numbers are particularly associated with that question.

And a similar thing happens with stereotypes. The model learns associations that occur frequently in human language, including our biases. So even if the prompt sounds neutral, that doesn’t mean the distribution of answers will be neutral. The model can fall back on a very familiar, stereotypical continuation. Fluency makes it easy to overlook that distinction: producing a plausible answer isn’t the same as following the underlying intent of the question.

r001.rationale: It says the model predicts likely text from training patterns, and that some numbers appear more often than others, explaining why outputs are not evenly random.

r002.rationale: It mentions learned associations and familiar stereotypical continuations, but does not say post-training concentrates output probabilities or that this reflects answers people prefer.
